opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think debugging is one of the most underrated skills right now, and honestly it's becoming more important, not less, as agents get more capable.

When you're working with an agent, you're no longer writing every line yourself. You're delegating, and the agent produces a lot of output very quickly. That's great when it works. But when something goes wrong, and it will, you need to figure out *why*, and the "why" is often buried several layers deep. Did the model misunderstand the instruction? Did it get bad context? Did a tool return something unexpected? Did it make a reasonable assumption that happened to be wrong for your situation? Those are all different failure modes with different fixes, and if you can't tell them apart, you end up just rerunning the thing and hoping.

What I've noticed is that the people who get the most out of agents tend to be the ones who are good debuggers in the classic sense. They form hypotheses, they isolate variables, they read the actual logs and traces instead of guessing. They treat the agent's behavior as something you can investigate rather than something mysterious. And that mindset carries over really well, because an agent is basically a system with inputs, intermediate state, and outputs, and you can reason about it the same way you'd reason about any other system.

There's also a trust piece. If you can't debug what an agent did, you can't really verify it, and if you can't verify it, you either over-trust it, which is dangerous, or you under-trust it and redo everything by hand, which defeats the purpose. Debugging is what lets you hit that middle ground where you're confident in the output because you know how to check it.

And the last thing I'd say is that debugging builds intuition. Every time you trace a failure back to its root cause, you learn something about how these models behave, where they're strong, where they tend to slip. Over time that makes you better at setting them up to succeed in the first place: better prompts, better context, better guardrails. So it's not just a recovery skill, it's really how you get good at working with agents at all.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses agents producing output quickly and sometimes going wrong, but does not say an agent can perform brilliantly while missing a crucial detail that invalidates its work.

r002.rationale: The candidate says people need to debug and verify agent output, but does not identify distinguishing adequate answers from excellent ones as a fundamental human responsibility.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss the abundance of coding jobs or attribute it to the knowledge and skill needed to operate AI tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think debugging is maybe the single most underrated skill in this whole space, and the reason is that working with an agent is fundamentally a debugging loop, whether or not people recognize it as one.

When you hand a task to an agent and it comes back with something that's not quite right, you're in exactly the position a programmer is in when a test fails. You have a system that did something, you have an expectation of what it should have done, and there's a gap. The question is how you close that gap. And people who've spent years debugging software have a set of instincts that transfer almost perfectly. You don't just stare at the output and guess. You form a hypothesis about where things went wrong. You isolate variables. You ask, was it the instruction that was ambiguous, was it missing context, did the model make a reasoning error partway through, or did it have the wrong tool available? Each of those has a different fix, and if you don't diagnose which one it is, you end up just rephrasing your prompt randomly and hoping.

The other piece is that agents fail in ways that are often invisible at the surface. The final answer can look plausible while the chain of steps that produced it was wrong in step three. Good debuggers are used to not trusting the surface. They go read the trace, they look at what the agent actually called, what it actually saw, and they find the moment where the state diverged from what they assumed. That habit of reading the actual execution rather than the summary is huge.

And honestly, there's a mindset component too. Debugging teaches you a kind of patience and humility. You learn that the system is doing exactly what it was told, and if the result is wrong, the most likely explanation is that your mental model of what you told it is off. That's incredibly healthy when working with agents, because the temptation is to anthropomorphize and get frustrated, when really you should be asking what information or structure you failed to provide. So I'd say if you want to get good at this, you don't need to learn some brand new discipline. You need to get really good at the thing programmers have been doing for sixty years, which is figuring out why a system didn't do what you expected.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent’s final answer can look plausible even when its execution went wrong, but it does not clearly describe brilliant performance undermined by a crucial missed detail.

r002.rationale: It presents debugging and diagnosing agent failures as useful human skills, but does not identify distinguishing adequate answers from excellent ones as a fundamental human responsibility.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss coding jobs or attribute their abundance to the knowledge and skill needed to operate AI tools.

astra-6.text:
I think debugging is valuable because working with an AI agent means working with a system that can do a lot, but whose mistakes aren’t always obvious. It might misunderstand the goal, make a bad assumption, or produce something that looks convincing but doesn’t actually work. You need to be able to figure out where things went wrong.

And debugging is really a way of thinking: What did I expect to happen? What actually happened? What evidence would help me distinguish between possible explanations? Can I isolate the problem and test it? Those habits are useful even if you’re not writing code.

As agents take on more of the execution, being able to evaluate their work and give them precise feedback becomes more valuable. “This is wrong” doesn’t give an agent much to work with. “Here’s the case that fails, here’s what I expected, and here’s the assumption I think we need to revisit” gives you a much better chance of making progress.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can produce convincing work that does not actually work because it misunderstood the goal or made a bad assumption, conveying capable output undermined by a subtle failure.

r002.rationale: It says people should evaluate agents’ work and give precise feedback, but does not identify distinguishing adequate answers from excellent ones as a fundamental human responsibility.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss coding jobs or attribute their abundance to the knowledge and skill needed to use AI tools effectively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think debugging is valuable because working with agents means dealing with systems that don’t always do what you expect. You need to be able to look at a result and ask, “Where did this go wrong?” Did the agent misunderstand the goal? Was it missing information? Did it use a tool incorrectly, or fail to check its work?

That’s a debugging mindset: breaking a problem down, forming a hypothesis, and testing it instead of just changing the prompt and hoping for a better answer. And as agents take on longer tasks, that becomes more important. You can delegate the execution, but you still need to understand enough about the process to recognize failures and help correct them.
